question.text: This 1854 act created the two namesake territories and allowed them to decide whether to become slave states using the doctrine of popular sovereignty.
question.clue: Josiah Miller and R.G. Elliott organized the Sandbank Convention as a consequence of the passage of this act, which also stimulated the activity of the Emigrant Aid Company.

swap.leadin: This man was shot and killed by a Union soldier after the barn where he was hiding was set on fire.
swap.text: Name this stage actor who shouted "Sic semper tyrannis" as he assassinated Abraham Lincoln.
swap.clue: Samuel Mudd created a splint for this man's broken leg.

question.leadin: Name some 19th Century Supreme Court cases.
question.text: Involving a slave who claimed he should no longer be a slave as his master transported him to a free territory, this 1857 case held that slaves were property and blacks were not citizens.
question.clue: Benjamin Curtis, who also dissented, claimed that the decision ignored citizenship rights granted by the Articles of Confederation.

swap.leadin: Give the following about the American West.
swap.text: This 1862 act gave about 160 acres of land to those who lived on and improved the land for five years.
swap.clue: This act, whose first beneficiary was Daniel Freeman, led to many people moving west to territories such as Oklahoma.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the Civil War.
question.text: This man replaced General McClellan as the Commander of the Army of the Potomac. He fought at the Battle of Fredericksburg and stormed his namesake bridge at Antietam.
question.clue: This first president of the NRA led the failed Mud March in an attempt to capture Richmond.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the merchant Wilmer McLean and his unique role in the Civil War.
swap.text: McLean's house was used as the headquarters for this Confederate general during the First Battle of Bull Run. His order to fire at Fort Sumter began the Civil War.
swap.clue: Near the end of the Civil War, he was given command of the Department of the West, but clashed with John Bell Hood, failed to stall Sherman, and was replaced with Joseph Johnston.

question.text: In reaction to the raid on Lawrence, Kansas by border ruffians, Brown and local militia perpetrated this event, killing 5 pro-slavery settlers.
question.answerHtml: Pottawatomie Massacre [accept reasonable equivalents mentioning an attack in Pottawatomie]
question.clue: Henry Clay Pate briefly captured some of this event's perpetrators, but then surrendered to the others at the Battle of Black Jack.

swap.leadin: Name some things about trains and the Civil War.
swap.text: A.P. Hill's Confederates beat back Burnside's attack and saved the day at this battle after rushing over from taking the critical railroad bridge at Harper's Ferry. The Emancipation Proclamation was announced after this battle.
swap.clue: The carnage during this conflict earned a sunken road the moniker "Bloody Lane."

question.leadin: Answer the following about an American history.
question.text: Many Northern Know Nothings went back to the Republican Party after this 1856 Supreme Court case that declared Congress to have no power to prohibit slavery in the territories.
question.clue: One party believed that his position had a strong precedent set in Rachel v. Walker, and thus the time spent in Fort Armstrong in Illinois entitled him to relief.

swap.leadin: A popular, but likely inaccurate legend states that this man ate lemons whole in an attempt to cure his dyspepsia.
swap.text: Name this military man whose last words, "Let us cross over the river, and rest under the shade of the trees," may have been a reference to his West Virginian childhood.
swap.clue: This commander of the "foot cavalry" routed Joseph Hooker's right flank during a battle that saw the amputation of his left arm after it was accidentally shot by his own men.

question.text: The Bourbon Democrats opposed an 1890 Silver Purchase Act sponsored by a senator with this surname who also wrote a namesake Antitrust Act. Another man with this surname stated "if nominated, I will not accept; if elected, I will not serve" when asked to run for president.
question.clue: An act named for a person with this surname was passed simultaneously with the McKinley Tariff and replaced the earlier Bland-Allison Act.

swap.text: During Buchanan's presidency, Free-Staters and Border-Ruffians fought over the expansion of slavery during this conflict, which took place in a namesake territory.
swap.clue: The Free State Hotel was targeted by a side in this conflict.

question.leadin: This ship's rotating turret inspired her namesake "mania" in the 19th century.
question.text: Name this vessel that was made famous by an indecisive encounter with the CSS Virginia.
question.clue: So skeptical were officials about the seaworthiness of this vessel that all development costs were to be returned by its designer, John Ericsson, if it failed.

swap.leadin: On her first tour of Britain, this book's author was presented with 26 volumes containing half a million signatures of British women.
swap.text: Name this novel that encouraged resistance to the Fugitive Slave Act and prompted Lincoln to call its author, Harriet Beecher Stowe, "the little lady who made this big war."
swap.clue: Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote this sentimental novel about the horrors of slavery that led Abraham Lincoln to allegedly call her "the little woman who started the big war."

question.text: A member of this family adhered to the Common School movement and penned a series of essays urging female opposition to the Indian Removal Act. This New-England-based abolitionist family armed free soilers with their namesake "bibles" during "Bleeding Kansas."
question.clue: A family patriarch with this surname was the first president of the Lane Theological Seminary.

swap.text: The Iroquois soldier Ely Parker, a close friend of Ulysses S. Grant, was selected due to his perfect handwriting to draft the treaty that ended the Civil War at this Virginia town where Robert E. Lee surrendered.
swap.clue: This courthouse was the site of Lee's official surrender to Grant at the end of the war.

question.leadin: Name some historians of the Civil War.
question.text: This former Princeton professor wrote Battle Cry of Freedom, the definitive survey of the antebellum period and the Civil War.
question.clue: This Princeton historian wrote the Pulitzer Prize-winning book Battle Cry of Freedom: The Civil War Era. He shares his name with the Union commander of the Army of Tennessee who was killed during the Battle of Atlanta.

swap.leadin: Prior to this battle, the losing side had crossed the Rappahannock River, and instead of ordering a flanking maneuver, the losing general instead ordered six charges on defensive fortifications.
swap.text: Identify this Civil War battle of December 13, 1862, which resulted in about 12,500 Union casualties.
swap.clue: In this battle, the Union repeatedly charged Marye's Heights.

question.leadin: During this battle, Daniel McCook was killed as he shouted "Surrender, you traitors!" at the Dead Angle.
question.text: Name this tactical loss for the Union, the largest frontal assault by William Sherman against Confederates during the Atlanta Campaign.

swap.leadin: After the Civil War, this first commander of the Army of the Ohio ran the Green River Iron Company, which processed iron to make steel.
swap.text: Name this Union general who first made a name for himself in the Mexican-American War at Churubusco, but who is more notable for his arrival at Pittburg Landing, which helped Grant win Shiloh.
swap.clue: This Union general led the Army of the Ohio at Perryville. One of the few Union officers to own slaves, he was criticized for his caution following the battle. Despite his name, he was born in Ohio.
